quote: Die Convergenz findet warscheinlich genau so statt, nur dass die sich ergebenden unendlichen Reihen nicht die an- genäherte Function darstellen.
english: The convergence probably takes place in exactly the same way, except that the resulting infinite series do not represent the approximated function.
topic: The page discusses least-squares approximation over [-1,1] by polynomials plus sqrt(x^2-1) times polynomials, generalisations to other function systems and side conditions, literature on continued fractions, and begins a theorem about polynomials normalised by an integral, proved via spherical (Legendre) functions.

triage.modern_statement: Take a system of functions on [-1,1] (or a system with side conditions) that need not be complete. Form its least-squares (orthogonal) expansion of a function f: orthonormalise the system, or equivalently take the successive least-squares approximants. Hilbert's conjecture is that this expansion still converges in the same way as in the complete case (polynomials, or polynomials plus sqrt(x^2-1) times polynomials), but that when the system is not complete the limit is not f. In modern L2 terms, the partial sums converge to the orthogonal projection of f onto the closed span of the system. That projection equals f for every f exactly when the system is complete.
triage.answered_by: This was settled by the Hilbert-space theory built in the following decades (the Bessel inequality, Riesz–Fischer, and the projection theorem). The partial sums of an orthogonal expansion always converge in mean square to the projection onto the closed span, and they represent f only when the system is complete. For specific systems such as the powers x^{λ_n}, the completeness question was answered by Müntz (1914) and Szász (1916): the Müntz–Szász theorem. I could not determine which function system Hilbert had in mind, so matching the note to these results is my own interpretation.

evidence.claim: When an orthonormal sequence is complete, Bessel's inequality becomes Parseval's identity. Otherwise the expansion keeps only part of the function's energy, so it converges but need not reproduce f.
Standard Hilbert-space lecture notes: the Fourier–Bessel series built from any countable orthonormal set gives the orthogonal projection onto the closure of the set's span.

The Müntz–Szász theorem gives the condition for the monomials x^{λ_n} to be complete in L2 or in C[0,1]. The non-complete case, where approximation fails to represent the function, has its own literature.
A Springer lecture treats the non-completeness case of the Müntz–Szász theorem and Malliavin's theorem.

triage.why: Read in its most likely sense, the note says that least-squares expansions in a general, possibly incomplete, system converge but give the projection of f rather than f itself. That is now a standard textbook fact of L2 and Hilbert-space theory, not an open problem, and it is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. The note does not say which function system or side conditions Hilbert meant, so I cannot confirm this reading. If he meant pointwise or uniform convergence for a particular system, the answer would depend on that system. For specific systems, completeness questions (Müntz-type theorems and their generalisations) are still researched, but the general statement itself is settled.
